# Packages and functions

## What is a package?

A package is a bundle of tools that someone has written and shared to help you do specific kinds of work in R.

It usually contains:

-   Functions (the main thing you use)
-   Documentation (help files)
-   Sometimes example datasets

A package is like installing an “app” for R. Base R is what comes pre-installed and Packages are extra apps you download when you need new features

## What is a function?

A function is a named command that does a specific job.

You give it inputs → it does something → it gives you an output.

It is like a button on a calculator. You press “mean” → it computes the mean.

# Installing and Using Packages

## Installing a package

You can install a package by selecting the packages tab your console pane where you have Files, Plots, Packages, etc. Then click on the install icon at the top left. Start typing in the package you want to install. It will give you some autofill options, you can type the whole thing in or select it from the autofill options. Then click on 'Install'.

You can also run a simple line of code (which you can see in your R Console is what all the button clicking in the previous paragraph does).




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# package name must be in quotes
#install.packages("tidyverse")

# after you have installed the package you do not need to install it again
```
:::




You only run the `install.packages()` function for a given package one time and then once the package is installed you should not run this line of code again. Either comment it out or delete it. Now you have a copy of the package saved on your computer.

## Loading packages

Once a package is installed you need to load it. This makes the package available in your current R session.

I highly recommend creating a setup code chunk at the beginning of each of your Quarto documents where you load in all of the packages that you will need. If you load an additional package later in the document, circle back around and add it to your setup chunk.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#set this to suppress a warning or message when you run a chunk
#| warning: FALSE 
#| message: FALSE

library(tidyverse)
```
:::




Today we are specifically going to be talking about the package `dplyr` which is useful to manipulating data sets.

# `can_lang` dataset

In this class, we are going to be working with a dataset relating to the languages spoken at home by Canadian residents. Many Indigenous peoples exist in Canada with their own languages and cultures. Sadly, colonization has led to the loss of many of these languages. This data is a subset of data collected during the 2016 census.

# Importing Data

What is a .csv file?

How do we import it into R?

Use `read_csv()`! Note that your data file (`.csv`) needs to be saved in the same folder as your notes template document (`.qmd`).

::: callout-tip
There is another function called `read.csv`, don't use it. Using `read_csv` will save you a lot of headaches in the long run. They work slightly differently and `read_csv` does a better job interpreting different data types and assigning classes correctly when reading in data. You may not understand what this means right now, but trust me, it will matter later.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use ?read_csv to look at the help documentation
# assigning a whole data frame to an object names can_lang
#can_lang <- read_csv("./data/can_lang.csv") 

# my filepath might look different from yours, you need to direct R
# to where you put your file, don't just copy my path

# absolute filepath to the location of can_lang.csv on my computer
can_lang <- read_csv("~/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/my_class_website/courses/STAT118/notes/published/data/can_lang.csv") # yours

# relative filepath to the same thing
can_lang <- read_csv("./courses/STAT118/notes/published/data/can_lang.csv")


# if you have used the file structure I have given you
# then your filepath should simply be:
# "data/can_lang.csv"
```
:::




Alternatively, you can download it directly from the internet. Github user `ttimbers` hosts this file to share with the public at the link: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ttimbers/canlang/master/inst/extdata/can_lang.csv>

## `filter()`

We can use the `filter` function to extract ***rows*** from the data that match a certain condition or set of conditions.

We define the condition with a logical expression using the logical operators are given below:

| Operator | Description              |
|----------|--------------------------|
| `<`      | Less than                |
| `>`      | Greater than             |
| `<=`     | Less than or equal to    |
| `>=`     | Greater than or equal to |
| `==`     | Equal to                 |
| `!=`     | Not equal to             |
| `!x`     | Not x                    |
| `x | y`  | x OR y                   |
| `x & y`  | x AND y                  |

For example, we may be interested in only looking at only the languages in this dataset that are Aboriginal languages.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# ?filter() for help documentation
# wants data and an expression that returns a logical value

can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages")
```

## `mutate()`

`mutate()` creates new columns that are functions of existing variables.

For example, if I want to create a new column called `mother_tongue_K` which represents the number of people who speak the language their mother tongue in thousands. You may want to save this new dataset over top of the original dataset so you could use this new column in the future.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# make a column of all 5


# mutate on column of mother_tongue/1000


# do the same thing as above but add a column of 1000 and then do the math with the columns


# add multiple columns together
```
:::




This can be useful for unit conversions. It also be useful for making new calculations based on existing data (for example, price and number of square feet could be used to calculate price per square foot).


# Making sure things actually print out in your assignment

There are various ways to make sure that your answers in your assignment actually print out in the rendered document. 

The output of a series of pipes will print out automatically unless you save it to a new object. 

You can have the first few rows print out using the `head()` function. You can also just call the object by name, which will create a printed output that will vary depending on the type of object. 

In your assignments you will be expected to have printed output or written answers to all of the questions. Please proofread your html document once it is rendered and before submitting it.
